items.prompt: A friend made plans on your behalf; you don't want to go, but saying no might hurt them. What do you say?

options.text: You thank them, say you can't join, and clearly explain why.
You gently say you won't join and leave the reason mostly unsaid.
You suggest an alternative time; you keep your decision clear but soft.
You go along for now; later, alone, you note how you felt and clarify it for yourself.

items.prompt: In a meeting your idea was cut off; you want the floor again. The room is competitive. What do you do?

options.text: You politely ask for the floor and finish your point.
You type in chat that you'd like to continue, then take the floor.
You wait until the topic moves on, then add a short note.
You stay silent and let the unfinished part go.

items.prompt: Your partner keeps changing plans at the last minute; you want to respond. Over time, what do you do?

options.text: You say the changes are hard for you and ask for earlier notice. This may cost time or clarity.
You explain with examples when you can be flexible and when you can't. You weigh short-term ease against longer-term balance.
You mention it once, then adapt again. This may cost time or clarity.
You treat it as normal and don't complain. You weigh short-term ease against longer-term balance.

items.prompt: At a family gathering, a topic that bothers you comes up again. It was always redirected before. What do you do this time?

options.text: You calmly but clearly say you don't want to discuss this topic.
You briefly explain why it bothers you and suggest another topic.
You try to change the subject again without saying it directly.
You brush it off; to avoid tension, you keep your boundary quiet for now.

items.prompt: A coworker keeps messaging outside work hours. The pattern is wearing you down. How do you approach it?

options.text: You clarify that you won't reply after hours and define what counts as urgent.
You say you're tired and that you'll reply the next day.
You still answer most messages, but with a delay.
To protect the relationship, you reply to every message immediately.

items.prompt: Someone you're dating often wants to drop by unplanned; you want to keep your schedule. In the repeating pattern, what do you do?

options.text: You propose a shared visit rhythm and clarify which days work.
You name your flexible days and remind them you're busy on others.
You struggle to say no and often rearrange your schedule.
You try to keep distance without saying it bothers you.

items.prompt: Your roommate uses shared space differently and it bothers you. You haven't talked yet. What's your first move?

options.text: You set aside a good time to talk about shared rules.
You send a short message naming the discomfort and suggest talking in person.
You suggest postponing; you'll talk more clearly once things cool down.
You ask for a short break, gather yourself, then come back later.

items.prompt: Two friends start arguing in front of you. Do you tend to mediate or stay neutral?

options.text: You try to help both feel heard and calm things down. You also consider the relationship dynamic.
Without taking sides, you suggest tabling it for later. You weigh short-term ease against longer-term balance.
You listen without intervening. You weigh short-term ease against longer-term balance.
You leave the room and let it run its course. You also consider the relationship dynamic.

items.prompt: A team disagreement is growing at work; you see a different solution. How do you join the meeting?

options.text: You present your alternative with reasons and open dialogue.
You briefly name your concern and ask what others think.
You shorten the debate; before proposing a middle ground, you take the temperature.
You push back harshly in front of colleagues.

items.prompt: In a tense team meeting, a colleague can't hold back tears. What's your first impulse?

options.text: You suggest a short break to soften the room and keep your tone calm.
You steer the meeting toward picking the topic up later.
You continue the discussion, figuring feelings will settle with time.
You find it uncomfortable, change the subject, and overlook the emotion.

items.prompt: While texting someone you're dating, you suddenly feel tension. How do you handle the feeling before you write?

options.text: You pause a few minutes, name what you feel, then reply. You also consider the relationship dynamic.
You rewrite the message to soften the tone. You weigh short-term ease against longer-term balance.
You reply quickly, then realize it wasn't needed. You also consider the relationship dynamic.
You write exactly what you feel, accepting you may regret it. You weigh short-term ease against longer-term balance.

items.prompt: You got criticized at work; it's still sitting with you at lunch. Before the afternoon meeting, what do you do?

options.text: You take a short walk or breathing exercise to settle the feeling.
You find one useful takeaway from the feedback and focus there.
You push the feeling down and try to look professional.
You enter the meeting still replaying the criticism and struggle to focus.

items.prompt: Someone you just met starts sharing something personal. You're considering sharing a similar experience. What do you do?

options.text: You tell your experience openly and share how you felt.
You summarize your experience without giving every detail.
You listen supportively without sharing your own story.
You keep the conversation more general and avoid personal detail.

items.prompt: Your partner wants you to share your feelings; you usually don't open up much. How do you act tonight?

options.text: You try to honestly describe what you felt today.
You name one or two feelings, then move on without going deeper.
You say you're fine and don't go into detail.
You shift the conversation to another topic.

items.prompt: In a friend group, someone describes a hard stretch. You've lived something similar but don't want to share it in front of everyone.

options.text: You still briefly share your experience to support the group.
You offer to talk privately later and listen for now.
You stay supportive but don't share your own story.
You lighten the topic and try to cheer the room up.

items.prompt: A close friend is going through a hard breakup and texts about their feelings. You have other plans tonight but want to hear them. What do you do?

options.text: You postpone your plans, listen on the phone for a long time, and try to reflect their feelings.
You send a short, warm message and offer to talk in person tomorrow.
You send a practical tip list and add an example from your own experience.
You say you're busy and suggest an activity to distract them.

items.prompt: After an argument, a coworker is cold toward you; you want to make peace but still feel hurt. How do you take the first step?

options.text: You try to understand their view and ask directly how they feel. You weigh short-term ease against longer-term balance.
You wait a bit; once things cool, you offer a short apology and look for common ground. You also consider the relationship dynamic.
You keep things professional by tying talk back to work. You also consider the relationship dynamic.
You protect being right and keep the distance. You weigh short-term ease against longer-term balance.

items.prompt: Someone you're dating wants to open an emotional topic, but you're tired. What they want to share might affect you too. How do you respond?

options.text: Even though you're tired, you say you're ready to listen and give your attention.
You say you want to listen but prefer to keep it short.
You suggest a better time tomorrow and add a short supportive message.
You downplay the topic and try to steer elsewhere.

items.prompt: A friend criticizes you about an invitation you already declined. You consider why they might feel hurt — what's your first inner reaction?

options.text: Maybe they felt unimportant; you remember the invite mattered to them.
You think both sides may have a point and there may have been a communication gap.
You hear their reason but briefly state your priority too.
You summarize from your angle and ask about their context later.

items.prompt: In a team meeting a colleague stayed quiet. Later you notice their idea was overlooked. If you were in their place, what might you feel?

options.text: You think they may have felt invisible and disrespected.
You assume they may not have wanted to speak, yet still felt left out.
You note in general that the meeting dynamic didn't invite everyone equally.
You treat the silence as their choice and don't over-interpret.

items.prompt: In a friend group someone joked; another person didn't laugh and the room tensed. What might be going on for the person who didn't laugh?

options.text: They may have found the joke hurtful or felt targeted.
Their attention may have drifted, or their humor style may differ.
You briefly note they may have felt group pressure.
You think they may be overreacting and close the topic.

items.prompt: You realize you sent a harsh message to a friend; they haven't replied yet. What do you do?

options.text: You apologize, explain your intent, and say you want to talk.
You send a short follow-up that softens the message.
You wait, hoping time will fix it on its own.
You leave the message alone, believing you were right.

items.prompt: You argued with your partner and didn't speak overnight. What do you do in the morning?

options.text: You reopen contact with a calm message or coffee invite. You also consider the relationship dynamic.
You start with an apology or common-ground line. You weigh short-term ease against longer-term balance.
Until they move first, you act normal and don't bring it up. You also consider the relationship dynamic.
Still feeling right, you keep your distance. You also consider the relationship dynamic.

items.prompt: A misunderstanding left a coworker hurt with you. This has happened before. What do you usually do?

options.text: You clarify the misunderstanding and apologize or explain. You weigh short-term ease against longer-term balance.
You send a short check-in and plan to talk in person. You weigh short-term ease against longer-term balance.
You don't intervene, figuring it will pass. You also consider the relationship dynamic.
You leave all responsibility with the other person. You weigh short-term ease against longer-term balance.

items.prompt: Your partner seems distant today; you're tense and don't fully know why. Looking inward, what do you notice first?

options.text: You notice you took their behavior personally and your anxiety rose.
You think fatigue and stress are amplifying your reaction.
You can't name a clear emotion yet, but you know you're uncomfortable.
Because the issue seems to be with your partner, you don't examine your own state.

items.prompt: In a social setting you suddenly want to withdraw. How do you make sense of what might be underneath?

options.text: You notice social fatigue or a triggered memory may be involved.
You think the room is loud and your limits are filling up.
You simply say your mood is low without going deeper.
You blame the setting and don't question yourself.

items.prompt: After a heavy day, a small comment made you disproportionately angry. What do you tell yourself about the size of that reaction?

options.text: You notice accumulated stress magnified the reaction.
You accept the topic may have hit a sensitive spot for you.
You treat the anger as justified and don't examine your role.
You assume the other person was deliberately provoking you.

items.prompt: At a gathering you notice someone sitting alone while others chat in a group. How do you read the room?

options.text: You think they aren't being included and may feel left out.
You assume they may be tired or looking for someone familiar, and you're not sure yet.
You stay focused on your own conversation without much interpretation. You also consider the relationship dynamic.
You treat it as preference and don't pay attention. You also consider the relationship dynamic.

items.prompt: In a friend group, after someone joked you feel the room tense. What do you notice?

options.text: You think someone may have misread or been hurt by the joke.
You sense the humor didn't fit the moment. You also consider the relationship dynamic.
You assume it was just a brief silence and don't load much meaning onto it.
You don't notice the tension and keep chatting. You also consider the relationship dynamic.

items.prompt: You joined a new work team and notice who speaks up and who stays in the background. What's your first impression?

options.text: You think formal hierarchy and informal groups shape who participates.
You note that some topics pull certain people in more.
You notice the room's tension but still proceed with your own plan.
You note social cues but watch without intervening directly.
